title: The commonwealth of the Hebrews
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα βουλόμενος κατασκευάζειν ὅτι μηδὲν τῶν προειρημένων παρ᾿ αὐτῷ ζῴων διαφέρουσιν Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Χριστιανοί φησιν Ἰουδαίους ἀπ᾿ Αἰγύπτου δραπέτας γεγονέναι, μηδὲν πώποτε ἀξιόλογον πράξαντας, οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐν ἀριθμῷ αὐτούς ποτε γεγενημένους. περὶ μὲν οὖν τοῦ μὴ δραπέτας αὐτοὺς γεγονέναι μηδ᾿ Αἰγυπτίους ἀλλ᾿ Ἑβραίους ὄντας παρῳκηκέναι ἐν τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ, ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἡμῖν λέλεκται· εἰ δὲ τὸ μήτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ μήτ᾿ ἐν ἀριθμῷ αὐτοὺς γεγονέναι κατασκευάζεσθαι νομίζει ἐκ τοῦ μὴ πάνυ τι τὴν περὶ αὐτῶν ἱστορίαν εὑρίσκεσθαι παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησι, φήσομεν ὅτι εἴ τις ἐνατενίσαι τῇ ἀρχῆθεν αὐτῶν πολιτείᾳ καὶ τῇ τῶν νόμων διατάξει, εὕροι ἂν ὅτι γεγόνασιν ἄνθρωποι σκιὰν οὐρανίου βίου παραδεικνύντες ἐπὶ γῆς· παρ᾿ οἷς οὐδὲν ἄλλο θεὸς νενόμιστο ἢ ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι, καὶ οὐδεὶς τῶν εἰκόνας ποιούντων ἐπολιτεύετο. οὔτε γὰρ ζωγράφος οὔτ᾿ ἀγαλματοποιὸς ἐν τῇ πολιτείᾳ αὐτῶν ἦν, ἐκβάλλοντος πάντας τοὺς τοιούτους ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς τοῦ νόμου, ἵνα μηδεμία πρόφασις ᾖ τῆς τῶν ἀγαλμάτων κατασκευῆς, τοὺς ἀνοήτους τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπισπωμένης καὶ καθελκούσης ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς γῆν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς ψυχῆς. ἦν οὖν παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς νόμος καὶ τοιοῦτος· „μὴ ἀνομήσητε καὶ ποιήσητε ὑμῖν ἑαυτοῖς γλυπτὸν ὁμοίωμα, πᾶσαν εἰκόνα ὁμοίωμα ἀρσενικοῦ ἢ θηλυκοῦ, ὁμοίωμα παντὸς κτήνους τῶν ὄντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὁμοίωμα παντὸς ὀρνέου πτερωτοῦ, ὃ πέταται ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν, ὁμοίωμα παντὸς ἑρπετοῦ, ὃ ἕρπει ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὁμοίωμα παντὸς ἰχθύος, ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν τοῖς ὕδασιν ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς.“ καὶ ἐβούλετό γε ὁ νόμος τῇ περὶ ἑκάστου ἀληθείᾳ ὁμιλοῦντας αὐτοὺς μὴ ἀναπλάσσειν ἕτερα παρὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ψευδόμενα τὸ ἀληθῶς ἀρσενικὸν ἢ τὸ ὄντως θηλυκὸν ἢ τὴν κτηνῶν φύσιν ἢ τὸ ὀρνέων ἢ τὸ ἑρπετῶν γένος ἢ τὸ ἰχθύων. σεμνὸν δὲ καὶ μεγαλοφυὲς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὸ „μὴ ἀναβλέψας εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἰδὼν τὸν ἥλιον καὶ τὴν σελήνην καὶ τοὺς ἀστέρας, πάντα τὸν κόσμον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, πλανηθεὶς προσκυνήσῃς αὐτοῖς καὶ λατρεύσῃς αὐτοῖς.“ οἵα δὲ πολιτεία ἦν ὅλου ἔθνους, παρ᾿ ᾧ οὐδὲ φαίνεσθαι θηλυδρίαν οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν. θαυμαστὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ τὰ τῶν νέων ὑπεκκαύματα, τὰς ἑταίρας, ἀναιρεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς πολιτείας αὐτῶν. ἦν δὲ καὶ δικαστήρια τῶν δικαιοτάτων καὶ ἀπόδειξιν ὑγιοῦς βίου πολλῷ δεδωκότων χρόνῳ, πιστευομένων τὰς κρίσεις· οἵτινες διὰ τὸ καθαρὸν ἦθος καὶ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον ἐλέγοντο εἶναι θεοὶ πατρίῳ τινὶ Ἰουδαίων ἔθει. καὶ ἦν ἰδεῖν ἔθνος ὅλον φιλοσοφοῦν, καὶ διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ ἀκούειν τῶν θείων νόμων σχολὴν τὰ καλούμενα σάββατα καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἱερέων καὶ θυσιῶν, μυρία σύμβολα περιεχουσῶν τοῖς φιλομαθοῦσι σαφηνιζόμενα;
pass_a_gloss: After these, wishing to establish (κατασκευάζω) that Jews and Christians differ (διαφέρω) in nothing from the animals (ζῷα) previously named by him, he says that Jews became runaways (δραπέται) from Egypt, having never done anything noteworthy (ἀξιόλογον), never having been either in account (λόγος) or in number (ἀριθμός). About their not having been runaways nor Egyptians but, being Hebrews, having sojourned (παροικέω) in Egypt, it has been said by us above. But if he thinks their having been neither in account nor in number is established from their history (ἱστορία) not being found much among the Greeks, we will say that if anyone gazed intently (ἐνατενίζω) at their commonwealth (πολιτεία) from the beginning and the ordering (διάταξις) of the laws, he would find that they were men displaying (παραδείκνυμι) a shadow (σκιά) of heavenly (οὐράνιος) life on earth; among whom nothing else had been held (νομίζω) God except the one over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι), and none of those making images (εἰκόνες) was a citizen (πολιτεύομαι). For neither painter (ζωγράφος) nor statue-maker (ἀγαλματοποιός) was in their commonwealth, the law expelling (ἐκβάλλω) all such from it, so that there might be no pretext (πρόφασις) for the making (κατασκευή) of statues (ἀγάλματα), which draws in (ἐπισπάω) the senseless (ἀνόητοι) of men and drags down (καθέλκω) the eyes of the soul (ψυχή) from God to earth. There was then among them also such a law: 'do not act lawlessly (ἀνομέω) and make for yourselves a carved (γλυπτός) likeness (ὁμοίωμα), any image, likeness of male or female, likeness of any beast (κτῆνος) of those on the earth, likeness of any winged bird (ὄρνεον πτερωτόν) which flies under heaven, likeness of any creeping thing (ἑρπετόν) which creeps on the earth, likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth.' And the law wished (βούλομαι) them, conversing with (ὁμιλέω) the truth (ἀλήθεια) about each, not to fashion (ἀναπλάσσω) other things beside the truth, falsifying (ψεύδομαι) the truly male or the really female or the nature of beasts or the kind (γένος) of birds or of creeping things or of fish. Solemn (σεμνός) and lofty (μεγαλοφυής) among them also the [precept]: 'not having looked up to heaven and seen the sun and moon and stars, all the order (κόσμος) of heaven, having been led astray (πλανάω) shall you bow to (προσκυνέω) them and serve (λατρεύω) them.' And what sort of commonwealth was [that] of a whole nation (ἔθνος), among which not even an effeminate man (θηλυδρίας) could appear. Wonderful (θαυμαστός) also the removal (ἀναιρέω) from their commonwealth of the incentives (ὑπεκκαύματα, 'kindlings') of the young, the courtesans (ἑταῖραι). There were also courts (δικαστήρια) of the most just, who had given proof (ἀπόδειξις) of a sound (ὑγιής) life over much time, entrusted (πιστεύω) with the judgments (κρίσεις); who on account of the pure (καθαρός) character (ἦθος) and the above-human were called gods by some ancestral (πάτριος) custom (ἔθος) of the Jews. And it was [possible] to see a whole nation philosophising (φιλοσοφέω), and on account of the leisure (σχολή) for hearing the divine laws the so-called sabbaths (σάββατα) and the remaining [feminine noun, unexpressed] among them of priests (ἱερεῖς) and sacrifices (θυσίαι), containing (περιέχω) countless symbols (σύμβολα) made clear (σαφηνίζω) to the lovers of learning (φιλομαθεῖς)?
pass_b_english: After this, wishing to establish that Jews and Christians differ in no way from the creatures he named earlier, he says that “the Jews were runaways from Egypt, who never did anything worth mentioning, and were never of any account or number.” Now, that they were not runaways, nor Egyptians, but Hebrews who lived as sojourners in Egypt, we have already said above. But if he thinks it is proved that they were “of no account or number” from the fact that their history is scarcely to be found among the Greeks, we will say that if anyone looks closely at their commonwealth from its beginning and at the ordering of their laws, he would find that they were men who showed on earth a shadow of the heavenly life.

Among them nothing else was held to be God but the One who is over all, and none of those who make images had a place among their citizens. For there was neither painter nor sculptor in their commonwealth, since the law banished all such people from it, so that there might be no occasion for the making of statues, which lures the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to earth. So they had a law such as this: “Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast of those that are on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, all that are in the waters beneath the earth” (Deuteronomy 4:16–18). Indeed, the law wished them to keep company with the truth about each thing and not to fashion other things contrary to the truth, counterfeiting what is truly male or really female, or the nature of beasts, or the kind of birds, of creeping things, or of fish.

Solemn and lofty, too, is their precept: “Do not, when you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the array of heaven, be led astray and bow down to them and serve them” (Deuteronomy 4:19). And what a commonwealth it was, that of a whole nation in which it was not even possible for an effeminate man to be seen! Wonderful, too, is the fact that the courtesans, who inflame the young, were removed from their commonwealth (Deuteronomy 23:17). They had courts made up of the most just men, men who had given proof of a sound life over a long time, to whom judgments were entrusted; and these, because of their pure character and what in them was more than human, were called gods, by an ancestral custom of the Jews. One could see a whole nation practising philosophy; and, to give leisure for hearing the divine laws, there were the so-called sabbaths and their other [ordinances], those of priests and of sacrifices, which contain countless symbols made clear to those who love learning.

The source row repeats 'οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ' twice (οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐν ἀριθμῷ); this is a dittography in the staged text and is translated once, as the phrase is repeated correctly later in this chapter and in 4.32. 'of no account or number' renders the proverbial οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐν ἀριθμῷ ('counted neither in esteem nor in number'). 'we have already said above' refers back to Origen's earlier answer on the Exodus (Book 3, opening chapters); no cross-reference number is given in the Greek. Deuteronomy 4:16-19 checked against LXX wording (ἀνομήσητε, γλυπτὸν ὁμοίωμα, ὀρνέου πτερωτοῦ, πάντα τὸν κόσμον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ); verse numbers are the same in LXX and English. Deuteronomy 23:17 (LXX 23:18: οὐκ ἔσται πόρνη ἀπὸ θυγατέρων Ισραηλ, καὶ οὐκ ἔσται πορνεύων ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ισραηλ) is the probable legal basis for both the effeminate man and the courtesans; cited once beside the courtesans; English numbering used. The judges 'called gods' probably reflects Exodus 22:28 (LXX 22:27, θεοὺς οὐ κακολογήσεις) and Exodus 21:6 / 22:8-9 LXX ('to the judgment-seat of God'), read of judges, or Psalm 82:6; Origen names only 'an ancestral custom', so this is left uncited. The last sentence is defective in the staged text: αἱ λοιπαί ... ἱερέων καὶ θυσιῶν has no feminine noun, and the sentence ends with a Greek question mark. A noun (perhaps 'feasts' or 'orders') seems to have dropped; the supplied word is bracketed as [ordinances] and should be checked against the printed Koetschau text. The question mark is not reproduced, since the sentence as staged has no question word; the sense is a statement of admiration. 'commonwealth' renders πολιτεία throughout (constitution and way of life of the people).
